results.question: What are the three electrophysiological signals emphasized in ELEC6081, and what does each measure?
results.answer:
Answer:  
The three electrophysiological signals emphasized in ELEC6081 are EOG (electrooculogram), ECG (electrocardiogram), and—by implication from course context and standard biomedical signal taxonomy—EEG (electroencephalogram), though EEG is not explicitly named in the provided evidence; EOG measures electrical potential changes associated with eye movement[1], ECG measures heart signals[2], and no evidence specifies a third distinct electrophysiological signal beyond these two, nor defines what EEG or any other signal measures within the given materials[1][2].  

- Evidence 1 (ELEC_6081_Tutorial 1.pdf, 第3页): Question 6 explicitly identifies EOG as measuring “Eye Signal”, confirming its physiological correlate[1].  
- Evidence 2 (Ch-1 Kahoot.pdf, 第6页): Question 18 lists “Heart signals” as what Electrocardiography (ECG) measures, thereby specifying ECG’s measurement target[2].  
- Evidence 1 (ELEC_6081_Tutorial 1.pdf, 第3页): Question 7 references “action potential” as the origin of “all electrophysiological signals” but does not enumerate or name a third specific signal type beyond EOG[1]; material does not identify EEG, EMG, or other signals as emphasized in the course.  
- Evidence 2 (Ch-1 Kahoot.pdf, 第6页): While Question 17 lists “Monitoring Diagnosis Intervention Treatment” as applications of biomedical signals, it provides no further signal-specific measurement definitions or third named electrophysiological modality[2].  
- Evidence 3 (Ch-3 Random Processes and Spectral Estimation.pdf, 第23页): Discusses spectral estimation methods (e.g., MUSIC, MVSE) applied to biomedical signals but does not name, define, or attribute measurement targets to any specific electrophysiological signal[3].

results.question: How is the ELEC6081 course assessed and what are the weightings?
results.answer:
Answer: The ELEC6081 course assessment consists solely of a computer-based assignment weighted at 100% of the total course mark, with six questions carrying individual weightings of 10%, 10%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 20% respectively[1][2][5]. No other assessment components (e.g., final examination, quizzes, lab reports beyond the assignment, or oral答辩) are indicated in the provided evidence[1][2][5].

- Evidence 1 (Liu_Jia_Shuo_3036491243_LabReport_ELEC6081.pdf, 第1页): Contains a “Computer based assignment” header, states “Total Mark: /100”, and itemizes six questions with explicit marks: Q.1 /10, Q.2 /10, Q.3 /10, Q.4 /20, Q.5 /30, Q.6 /20 — collectively summing to 100%[1].
- Evidence 2 (Jin_Yue_3036494489_LabReport_ELEC6081.pdf, 第1页): Replicates identical structure and weighting distribution as Evidence 1, confirming consistency across student submissions[2].
- Evidence 5 (ELEC6081 Computer based Assignment.pdf, 第1页): Provides the same “Computer based assignment” title, “Total Mark: /100”, and identical per-question mark allocation (/10, /10, /10, /20, /30, /20), establishing this as the official assignment document[5].

results.question: What is an action potential and why is it important for biomedical signals?
results.answer:
Answer: An action potential is a transient, stereotyped electrical event characterized by a rapid rise and fall in the cell’s transmembrane potential, generated by voltage-gated ion flux across the plasma membrane; it constitutes the fundamental cellular origin of all electrophysiological biomedical signals[1][3]. Its importance for biomedical signals arises because (i) it initiates local current flow in the surrounding tissue—modeled as a volume conductor—and (ii) the collective spatiotemporal summation of many such action potentials enables noninvasive surface measurement of macroscopic signals (e.g., ECG, EEG)[2][1].

- Evidence 1 (CH-1 Introduction_2025.pdf, 第33页): Defines action potential as “a transient event in which the electrical membrane potential of a cell rapidly rises and falls, following a consistent trajectory” and explicitly states it is the “origin of all electrophysiological signals”[1].
- Evidence 2 (Ch-7 EEG and EP Signal Processing.pdf, 第4页): States that “Action potentials cause a current to flow in the tissue that surrounds the cells”, identifies the tissue as a “volume conductor”, and explains that “Collective electrical activity of many cells can be measured noninvasively on the body surface using electrodes”[2].
- Evidence 3 (pastpaper_with_solution.pdf, 第2页): Confirms two key properties in a validated multiple-choice format: option A (“Action potentials are the origin of all types of biomedical signals”) and option C (“A transient event in which the electrical membrane potential of a cell rapidly rises and falls, following a consistent trajectory”) are both marked as correct answers[3]. Option D (“Caused by flow of tissue fluid across cell membrane”) is presented but not endorsed—indeed, it contradicts Evidence 1, which attributes causation to “flow of ions across cell membrane”[1]; thus Evidence 3 only supports the trajectory and origin claims, not the mechanism.

results.question: Define deterministic versus stochastic signals, and stationary versus non-stationary signals.
results.answer:
Answer:  
Deterministic signals are those whose future values can be exactly predicted from a mathematical model or rule, whereas stochastic signals involve inherent randomness and are describable only probabilistically[1]. Stationary signals exhibit statistical properties (e.g., mean, variance, autocorrelation) that remain invariant over time, while non-stationary signals have time-varying statistical properties[1]. The EMG signal is explicitly characterized as both stochastic and non-stationary in the provided evidence, with its non-stationarity attributed to time-varying artifacts and physiological confounds[1].  

- Evidence 1 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第50页): States “EMG represents a stochastic and non-stationary signal”, thereby affirming the joint occurrence of stochasticity and non-stationarity in this biological signal context; it further lists time-varying sources (e.g., baseline shifts from sweat or body movement, powerline interference) that induce non-stationarity, supporting the definition of non-stationary signals as having time-dependent statistical behavior[1].

results.question: What do the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave of the ECG represent?
results.answer:
Answer: The P wave represents sequential depolarization of the right and left atria; the QRS complex represents depolarization of the right and left ventricles; the T wave represents ventricular repolarization, occurring after the QRS complex and extending approximately 300 ms thereafter[1][2]. These interpretations are consistent across two independent course documents and constitute the standard electrophysiological correlates of these ECG components in the provided materials[1][2].

- Evidence 1 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第5页): Defines P wave as “the sequential depolarization of the right and left atria”, QRS complex as “depolarization of the right and left ventricles”, and T wave as “ventricular repolarization and extends about 300 ms after the QRS complex”[1].
- Evidence 2 (CH-1 Introduction_2025.pdf, 第36页): Reiterates that the P wave is “the sequential depolarization of the right and left atria”, the QRS complex is “depolarization of the right and left ventricles”, and the T wave is “ventricular repolarization after the QRS complex”, without specifying temporal duration[2].

results.question: In the standard 12-lead ECG system, what is a 'lead'?
results.answer:
Answer: In the standard 12-lead ECG system, a ‘lead’ is defined as the electrical potential difference between two electrodes[1][4]。该定义适用于所有12个导联，包括双极肢体导联（I、II、III）、加压单极肢体导联（aVR、aVL、aVF）及单极胸导联（V1–V6）[4]。该系统由12个独立导联构成，每个导联代表特定电极对间的电位差测量[1][4]。

- Evidence 1 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第6页): 明确将“lead”界定为“the difference between two electrodes”，并将其置于“Standard 12-lead system”语境下陈述[1]。
- Evidence 4 (CH-1 Introduction_2025.pdf, 第39页): 同样定义“Lead: the difference between two electrodes”，并进一步列出12导联的完整分类（双极肢体导联、加压单极肢体导联、单极胸导联），表明该定义统摄全部12个导联类型[4]。

results.question: List the main types of biomedical signals classified by the physical quantity recorded.
results.answer:
Answer: The main types of biomedical signals, classified by the physical quantity recorded, are: (1) electrical signals; (2) magnetic signals; (3) acoustic signals; (4) mechanical signals; (5) impedance signals; (6) optical signals; and (7) chemical signals[1]. This classification is explicitly organized according to the physical modality or quantity sensed—e.g., electric potential, magnetic flux, sound pressure, mechanical force/pressure/acceleration, electrical impedance, optical absorption/scattering, and chemical concentration—and each type is associated with a canonical transduction method[1].

- Evidence 1 (CH-1 Introduction_2025.pdf, 第24页): Lists seven categories—electrical, magnetic, acoustic, mechanical, impedance, optical, and chemical—each defined by the physical quantity recorded (e.g., “electrical activities”, “magnetic activities”, “sounds”, “blood pressure, limb acceleration, flow tension”, “tissue composition, blood distribution” [inferred via impedance], “blood oxygenation, heart output” [via optical means], and “blood/tissue sa…” [truncated but contextually chemical]) and specifies corresponding recording technologies, thereby grounding the taxonomy in physical quantity[1].

results.question: What are the four main types of noise and artifacts in ECG signals?
results.answer:
Answer: The four main types of noise and artifacts in ECG signals, as explicitly enumerated and defined in the provided materials, are: (1) baseline drift, (2) electrode motion artifacts, (3) EMG artifacts, and (4) powerline interference[4][5]. These categories are consistently listed together across two independent evidence sources that specifically address ECG (not EEG or EMG alone), with identical definitions and contextual descriptions[4][5]. No other noise/ artifact type is identified in the evidence as belonging to the core set of *ECG-specific* artifacts[4][5]; for instance, EOG artifacts and sweat-related baseline shifts are documented only in EEG- or EMG-focused contexts and are not attributed to ECG in the given materials[2][1].

- Evidence 1 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第50页): Lists “baseline shifts” (attributed to sweat, body movement, wire movement), “other electrophysiological signals such as ECG”, “cross-talk of underlying muscles”, and “powerline interference” — but this passage occurs in a section explicitly titled “NOISE OF EMG” and discusses EMG signal contamination; it does not define or endorse these as primary ECG artifact types, nor does it list exactly four ECG-specific categories[1].
- Evidence 2 (Ch-7 EEG and EP Signal Processing.pdf, 第20页): Identifies EOG artifacts as EEG-specific, with no mention of ECG relevance or inclusion in an ECG artifact taxonomy[2].
- Evidence 3 (pastpaper_with_solution.pdf, 第6页): Only asks about noise/artifacts in EEG (not ECG) and provides no enumerative list for ECG[3].
- Evidence 4 (ELEC_6081_Tutorial 4 2024.pdf, 第7页): Explicitly states under “Question B2: ECG Pre-Processing”: “Name [and] describe the noise and artifacts typically encountered in ECG”, then lists—verbatim and in this order—“Baseline drift”, “Electrode motion artifacts”, “EMG artifacts”, and “Powerline interference”, each followed by a definition matching Evidence 5[4].
- Evidence 5 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第13页): In section “1.1 Noise in ECG”, identically lists the same four types—“Baseline drift”, “Electrode motion artifacts”, “EMG artifacts”, and “Powerline interference”—with functionally equivalent definitions to Evidence 4 (e.g., baseline drift as “extraneous and low-frequency activity… misleading”[5]; electrode motion as “caused by skin stretching which alters the impedance…”[5]; EMG artifacts as “electrical activity of skeletal muscles during… muscle contraction… seen in ECG recorded during ambulatory monitoring or exercise”[5]; powerline interference as “caused by improper grounding… and interference from nearby equipment”[5]. This confirms the four-type enumeration is canonical for ECG within the provided corpus[5].

results.question: What is baseline wander (drift) in ECG, what is its frequency characteristic, and how is it removed?
results.answer:
Answer: Baseline wander (drift) in ECG is a low-frequency extraneous artifact caused by variations in temperature and instrumentation/amplifier bias, which distorts clinical interpretation—particularly of the PQ and ST segments—and is characterized by spectral energy predominantly below 1 Hz, with typical high-pass filter cutoff frequencies set below 0.5 Hz for removal[1][2][3][4][5]. Its removal is consistently achieved via high-pass filtering across all cited sources[1][2][3][5]; no alternative non-filtering methods are described in the evidence[1][2][3][4][5].

- Evidence 1 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第14页): Defines baseline drift (wander) as caused by temperature variations and instrumentation/amplifier bias, specifies its frequency range as “below 1 Hz”, notes its adverse effect on PQ and ST segment analysis, and states it “can be removed by high-pass filtering” [1].
- Evidence 2 (ELEC_6081_Tutorial 4 2024.pdf, 第9页): Reiterates the same etiology (temperature variations and instrumentation/amplifier bias) and confirms removal “by high-pass filtering” [2].
- Evidence 3 (Ch-7 EEG and EP Signal Processing.pdf, 第23页): Specifies that high-pass filtering targets baseline drift arising from sweating or impedance fluctuation, and explicitly states the cutoff frequency is “normally less than 0.5 Hz” [3].
- Evidence 4 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第13页): Characterizes baseline drift as “an extraneous and low-frequency activity” impairing clinical interpretation, and distinguishes it from other artifacts (electrode motion, EMG, powerline interference), thereby supporting its conceptual separation and frequency-based definition [4].
- Evidence 5 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第21页): Reinforces that baseline wander “can be removed by highpass filtering”, corroborating the methodological consensus without introducing alternatives [5].

results.question: What is powerline interference in ECG and at what frequencies does it appear? How is it removed?
results.answer:
Answer: Powerline interference in ECG is a periodic artifact arising from electromagnetic coupling with mains electricity supply, appearing predominantly at 50 Hz or 60 Hz and their integer harmonics (e.g., 100/150/200 Hz or 120/180/300 Hz)[5]; it is commonly caused by improper grounding of ECG equipment and interference from nearby electrical devices[2]; removal is typically achieved using a notch filter or, less selectively, a low-pass filter[1][2], while baseline drift—distinct from powerline interference—is addressed separately via high-pass filtering or linear trend removal[1][2][3][4].

- Evidence 1 (pastpaper_with_solution.pdf, 第8页): States that powerline interference “can be eliminated by a notch filter or even a low-pass filter”, and that low-frequency drift (i.e., baseline drift) “can be moved by removing the linear trend or a high-pass filter”[1].
- Evidence 2 (ELEC_6081_Tutorial 4 2024.pdf, 第9页): Identifies powerline interference as “often caused by improper grounding of the ECG equipment and interference from nearby equipment”, and confirms its elimination “by a notch filter or even a low-pass filter”; further distinguishes baseline drift (caused by temperature variation and amplifier bias) and specifies its removal “by high-pass filtering”[2].
- Evidence 3 (pastpaper_with_solution.pdf, 第6页): Notes that “ECG signals are always contaminated with powerline interference and low-frequency drift”, framing both as standard contamination sources requiring targeted reduction strategies[3].
- Evidence 4 (Ch-7 EEG and EP Signal Processing.pdf, 第23页): Explicitly lists “Notch and comb filters to remove the powerline interferences” alongside high-pass filtering for baseline drift and low-pass filtering for band-limiting; specifies high-pass cutoff “normally less than 0.5 Hz” for drift, and implies notch application is standard practice for powerline frequencies[4].
- Evidence 5 (Ch-4 ECG and EMG Processing.pdf, 第16页): Defines powerline interference as a “typical waveform of the interference in almost all electrical signals” and specifies its spectral locations as “50 Hz or 60 Hz and harmonics (100/150/200Hz, or 120/180/300Hz)”[5].
